records.answer: To get Cursor working with Ark, you need to add the Ark MCP server to Cursor. You can do this by copying the generated config from the Onboarding tab's 'Connect Claude Code (superpowers)' card into `.cursor/mcp.json`, either globally at `~/.cursor/mcp.json` or project-scoped at the repo root. The config should have the shape `{ "mcpServers": { "ark": { "type": "http", "url": "https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.mlops.pai.mypaytm.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <YOUR_KEY>" } } } }`. You can also add it through Cursor's own settings: find the MCP servers list and add an HTTP server named `ark`, with the URL ending in `/mcp` and the `Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_KEY>` header. Then, verify the connection by opening Cursor's MCP servers list and checking that `ark` shows as connected with its tools listed, or by asking Cursor to 'list ark computes' and watching a real answer come back. You can also test the key itself by calling `auth/whoami` against the control plane.

# Set up Cursor 
Cursor shows up in Foundry in two unrelated ways, and this page covers both.
The first is Cursor as your editor: it connects to the control plane's MCP server and gets the `ark` toolbox, so you can dispatch sessions, inspect flows and steer runs without leaving Cursor. The second is Cursor as a **runtime** , one of the harnesses Foundry dispatches agents onto, alongside the `claude-agent` and `pi-dev` families and their `-pi-inference` gateway variants. In that mode nobody is sitting in the editor at all: a stage runs on Cursor's agent SDK, on an EC2 box, a registered host or in a Kubernetes pod, and reports back like any other stage.
If you only want to drive Foundry from your editor, read to the end of Use it and then skip to Notes and gotchas. If you are running flows on the Cursor harness, the sections from Cursor as an agent harness onward are the ones you need.

## What works differently inside a cursor session 
Most of Foundry works unchanged. The differences are the places where Cursor's SDK has no equivalent of what `claude-agent` offers.
**Skills arrive as text, not as a system prompt.** The SDK's options carry no system-prompt parameter, so an agent's `skills:` are folded into a rules file the runtime writes at `.cursor/rules/ark.mdc` with `alwaysApply: true`. The file is added to the repo-local git exclude, and the runtime refuses to overwrite it if the repo already tracks that path.

bash

To remove it:
bash
    
    mv ~/.ark/bin/ark-real ~/.ark/bin/ark && rm -rf ~/.ark/cursor-bridge

## The one-click bridge for older hosts 
There is an installer that puts a small Node `@cursor/sdk` bridge on a Mac and wraps `ark` so that only `run-cursor` routes to it. It exists for one narrow case: an enrolled Mac whose `ark` binary predates the packaging fix and which you cannot upgrade yet.
Prefer installing a current binary. The bridge shadows the real one with its own SDK copy and its own frozen launcher, and that copy has already drifted: it does not pass inline subagent declarations through, so an agent that declares them loses them silently. Once `ark host doctor` reports the cursor line, retire the bridge with the revert command below.
If you still need it, download it to a file rather than piping it into a shell, so you can pin and read exactly what you run:

If you do not have Claude access, you can dispatch against the Cursor runtime with `CURSOR_API_KEY` set instead. Selecting a runtime does not change what the **workspace** requires, so a workspace that declares `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` still demands it on a Cursor run.

# Updating the Ark CLI & plugin 
The `ark` binary and the `ark-superpowers` Claude Code plugin ship from the control plane, so they move forward as the platform does. When a release lands you re-pull both: the CLI to pick up new commands and fixes, the plugin so Claude Code sees the current agents, flows, and skills. This page is the update path once you already have an account and a working `ark login`. If you have not set either up yet, start at [Getting Access + MCP](/onboarding/getting-access).

records.answer: You can update the Ark CLI and plugin by running the command `ark install-claude-code`, which reinstalls the `ark-superpowers` plugin and reads the token from your active context. Alternatively, you can use a script that downloads the CLI to a temp file, verifies it, and then moves it into place, while also re-adding the marketplace with the current token and installing the plugin. The script is safe to re-run, whether or not the plugin is already installed.

**my session is stuck at ready, what's going on?**

Give it a couple of minutes and retry -- a lot of the old stuck-forever behaviour is gone now and runs fail fast with a real reason. If everyone is seeing it at the same time, it's the platform, not you. [see: faq]

**i enrolled my compute but nothing's happening**

**getting ssh clone error while preparing workspace**

## How scope resolution works 
Secrets resolve **narrowest first** : user, then team, then tenant, and the first hit for each name wins. A team that sets nothing inherits the tenant default.
Two consequences worth knowing before you debug a missing secret:
  - Setting a value at **user** scope overrides team and tenant for your sessions only. That makes it the fastest way to unblock yourself while a shared value is being sorted out.
  - A team-scoped secret is matched by the team's canonical `tm-` id. A value stored against the team's name or slug will be visible in the UI and still not resolve at dispatch.

## Roles, and how a team comes online 
Onboarding a team comes down to one person. The platform team creates the accounts and gives one person a tenant-admin grant. From there that admin unlocks the rest for the team: they onboard everyone else, register the team's compute, and set the team's secrets, without the platform team in the loop for each step.

**how do i add someone to the tenant**

Send the user's email and team name to a tenant admin (listed on the Settings page under Your admins), and the platform team will create their account. Then you control what they can do by granting them roles with the ark grant command. [see: admin]

**why does my team secret keep getting overridden by tenant settings**

Secret resolution follows user → team → tenant order, with the first match winning; if your team sets nothing, it simply inherits tenant defaults. [see: admin]

**can i set jira_base_url at team scope**

No—never override infra values like JIRA_BASE_URL at team scope, as it creates invisible per-team configuration drift that makes Ark appear broken only for that team. [see: admin]

Account creation (Cognito login + tenant membership) is done by the platform team - send the email and team name (or a .csv for a whole team) to a tenant admin, listed on the **Settings** page under **Your admins**. Once the user exists, you control _what they can do_ with grants:

  - `/ark` replies "Your Slack account is not linked" → token expired or the DM didn't land; redo Steps 2–3

## How work flows

- **Jira ticket:** Work is created and tracked where the team already works.
- **Ark reads the ticket:** Ark pulls ticket context and linked docs, holds the credentials, and a planner agent drafts a plan.
- **Ark runs the work:** Coding, testing, code review and validation run on managed compute.
- **Ark opens a PR:** Ark creates or updates a PR and attaches the test evidence.
- **Ark updates Jira:** Progress, the PR link, the test result and the status go back to the ticket.
- **Deploy and monitor:** Deployment and monitoring agents take the next approved action.

### 0. Make Ark Reliable

**Goal:** Stop the outages before we add anything new.

- Stop 503s: credential-refresh grant for the weekly DB password rotation, plus event-consumer backpressure.
- Redis recovery, and managed EC2 or EKS instead of laptops.
- Team-scoped compute and credentials, with pre-flight prerequisite checks.
- Prevent an arkd disconnect from stranding a run; detect machine loss and recover.
- Do not kill a healthy long build, and surface no silent hangs.
- Pause and resume on a rate limit, and preserve work on every kill.
- Reduce UI polling, keep auth stable under load, and deliver Slack alarms.

**Done when:** No unannounced outage over 5 minutes, failures are fast and clear, arkd holds at normal load, healthy builds keep running, no silent hangs, the UI stays fast, no repeated logouts, no lost work, and alerts fire before users report.

# Creating EC2 compute 
An `ec2` compute is usually a machine Foundry owns end to end: it launches the instance in your AWS account, installs `arkd` on it over SSM, stops it when it goes idle, and terminates it when you destroy the row. The same kind can also adopt a box you already run, in which case Foundry installs `arkd` and nothing else, as below. That is the difference from [registering a machine you already own](/onboarding/registering-compute), where the box dials in and Foundry never touches its lifecycle.
You create it in one of two shapes. A **dedicated box** is a single named instance your team's sessions land on, which is what most teams start with. A **pool** is a blueprint that cuts a fresh instance per session up to a ceiling you set, which is what you want once several people dispatch at once. Both are covered below; the sizing, capacity, and trou

## Verify 
bash
    
    ark compute list
    ark compute show risk-devbox
    ark compute metrics risk-devbox
`show` reports the box's declared capacity, its current occupancy, and the sessions placed on it. `list` reports each target's architecture once the box has checked in, which is how you confirm an arm box came up as arm64.
None of that proves dispatch works. Finish by running a small session pinned to the target:
bash
    
    ark session start --flow bare-auto --compute risk-devbox --summary "compute smoke test"
`bare-auto` is a single-agent flow that needs no workspace, so it isolates the compute: if its stage starts running, the box was reachable and `arkd` launched an agent on it. Repeat with `--workspace <name>` to prove the box can also clone that workspace's repos, which is the other half of the placement rule.

A dispatch refused with the compute's architecture in the message means the workspace declares an `arch` the box does not have. `ark compute list` reports what the box actually is once it has checked in, which is often the first time anyone notices an `--arch arm` row on an x86 instance type or the reverse.
A row that stays `stopped` and never wakes on dispatch usually has no `instance_id`, meaning it was created but never provisioned. `ark compute show` shows it: run `ark compute provision` rather than waiting.
`compute '<name>' already exists` on create means the name is taken in this tenant, including by a row someone else made. Names are unique per tenant, not per person.

**why does my team secret keep getting overridden by tenant settings**

Secret resolution follows user → team → tenant order, with the first match winning; if your team sets nothing, it simply inherits tenant defaults. [see: admin]

records.answer: You can enroll a compute host on Ark by running the `ark-enroll-host.sh` script, which automates the enrollment process. Alternatively, you can use the `ark host enroll` command to enroll a machine on behalf of someone else. To do this, an admin mints the token by running `ark host enroll <name>` and reading it from the host file, then sends it to the machine's owner, who places it at `~/.ark/host/registered-host/<name>/token` and runs `ark host start` with no admin credential needed.

This is a packaging bug in the Ark binary, not a problem with your repo or your ticket. Update to a build past it. Two traps make the update look like it did not work:

records.answer: To set up a k8s compute pool for Ark, you need to create a pool with the `ark compute pool create` command or the `compute/pool/create` JSON-RPC endpoint, providing a config bag that includes the cluster, namespace, pod image, and resource limits. The `roleArn` and `externalId` are required for cross-account setup, and `capacity` is used to set the ceiling for the pool. The cluster ref, namespace, and image are checked for prerequisites. Additionally, you need to have the necessary permissions, such as `compute.admin`, and the Ark CLI signed in to your control plane. You should also configure your AWS CLI and `kubectl` for the account and cluster you are using. You can use the `ark compute pool create` command with options like `--kind k8s`, `--self`, `--namespace`, `--image`, `--control-plane-url`, `--cpu`, and `--memory` to create the pool.

A `k8s` compute is not a machine. It is a pool row holding the cluster, the namespace, the pod image and the pod's resource limits, and every dispatch cuts one pod from it for one session. The pod runs `arkd` as its main container and dials out to the control plane, so nothing reaches into your cluster: no inbound route, no `kubectl port-forward`, no kubeconfig read at dispatch time. An `ec2` compute is usually a machine Foundry owns end to end: it launches the instance in your AWS account, installs `arkd` on it over SSM, stops it when it goes idle, and terminates it when you destroy the row. ## Sizing 
Four numbers decide pod size and throughput, and none of them substitutes for another:
Field| What it sets  
---|---  
`config.resources`| The `arkd` container's request and limit, in Kubernetes units (`"2"` is two cores, `"500m"` half of one). Applies when the session declares no budget of its own  
workspace `resource_budget`| What actually sizes the pod on a real dispatch, so a workspace can outgrow the pool default  
`config.sidecarResources`| Charged once per declared service, plus one for DinD, in the same pod  
`config.capacity`| The admission ledger's ceiling for the whole pool row

1. Open the **Onboarding** tab in the Foundry web UI and click **Generate** on the **Connect Claude Code (superpowers)** card. This mints a fresh user key and gives you a `.mcp.json` block.
2. Copy the generated block or download the file. It looks like:
```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ark": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.mlops.pai.mypaytm.com/mcp",
      "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer <YOUR_KEY>"}
    }
  }
}
```
3. Place the file where Cursor can read it:
   * **Global** – save to `~/.cursor/mcp.json` to make `ark` available for every repo, **or**
   * **Project‑scoped** – save to `.cursor/mcp.json` at the root of the repo you are working on. (If the repo is one that Foundry checks out for a session, use the global file instead, because the runtime will refuse to start when a project‑scoped file is present.)
4. Alternatively, you can add the same entry via Cursor UI: Settings → Tools and Integrations → *Add MCP server*, name it `ark`, set the URL ending in `/mcp`, and add the `Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_KEY>` header.
5. Verify the connection:
   * Open Cursor’s **MCP servers** list and confirm `ark` appears with its tools (`agent`, `compute`, `flow`, `session_lifecycle`, `workspace`, …).
   * In Cursor, run a command like **"list ark computes"** and see a real answer.
   * For an independent check, run the RPC call:
```bash
curl -s https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.mlops.pai.mypaytm.com/api/rpc -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_KEY>" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"auth/whoami","params":{}}'
```
   The response should contain your email and a role of `member`, `admin`, `viewer` or `system-admin`.
6. Common pitfalls:
   * Do **not** use `localhost` for the URL – it must be the full `https://ark.internal…/mcp` address.
   * If you see an error about a `.cursor/mcp.json` or `.cursor/hooks.json` in the worktree, remove the project‑scoped file and use the global config instead.
   * If `auth/whoami` returns `"role":"worker"`, you used a machine token; mint a fresh user key from the onboarding UI.
Once these steps are done, Cursor will be able to dispatch Ark sessions, list computes, and let you steer flows directly from the editor.

Claude Code shows the MCP as *connected* but the tools list stays red because the API key the MCP is using was rejected. The connection test succeeds (the server is reachable), but the credential is stale, wrong tenant, or duplicated, so the server returns a *tools fetch failed* status. Fix it by getting a fresh key, updating the MCP registration, removing any duplicate entry, and restarting Claude Code.

1. Open the Ark web UI → Settings → API Keys → Create key (name it `mcp‑<yourname>`). Copy the key.
2. Verify the key works with a direct `auth/whoami` call:
```bash
curl -s https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.mlops.pai.mypaytm.com/api/rpc -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_KEY>" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"auth/whoami","params":{}}'
```
   You should see your email and a role of `member` or `admin`.
3. Update the MCP registration:
   *If you used the plugin*, re‑run the plugin one‑liner or `ark install-claude-code` (it reads the active `ark login` context).
   *If you used the project‑scoped snippet*, replace the entry:
```bash
claude mcp remove ark
claude mcp add --transport http ark \
  https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.mlops.pai.mypaytm.com/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_KEY>"
```
4. Run `claude mcp list` and ensure only a single `ark` registration remains (no duplicate `plugin:ark‑superpowers:ark`).
5. Restart Claude Code so the new registration is picked up; the tools list should turn green and `ark auth whoami` will confirm the correct identity.

The root cause is an invalid or duplicated API key; correcting the key and cleaning up duplicate registrations resolves the “connected → tools fetch failed” state.

# Updating the Ark CLI & plugin 
The `ark` binary and the `ark-superpowers` Claude Code plugin ship from the control plane, so they move forward as the platform does. When a release lands you re-pull both: the CLI to pick up new commands and fixes, the plugin so Claude Code sees the current agents, flows, and skills. This page is the update path once you already have an account and a working `ark login`. If you have not set either up yet, start at [Getting Access + MCP](/onboarding/getting-access).

# Getting Started with Ark 
You have an account and the `ark` MCP connected in Claude Code or Cursor. This page is the first run: it takes you from a connected editor to a session you dispatched, watched, and reviewed, in seven ordered steps. Every step is a small command you can run and read the answer to, so you are never guessing whether the last one worked.
The four nouns everything is built from are a **compute** (where a run happens), a **workspace** (your project made real: repos, tools, secrets, actions), a **flow** (the delivery process written down as stages), and a **session** (one run of a flow on a workspace on a compute). Steps 2 through 4 pick each of the first three; step 5 puts them together into a session.

## 7\. Claude / models 
**7.1 "It says Claude rate limit reached / fleet auth quota exhausted."** You're sharing a quota that got throttled. Fix: use your own Claude token. Run `claude setup-token`, then add `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` as a User secret. Your sessions will use your token from then on. Team-level keys and Pi-Inference are the other options. If the error names a reset time (e.g. `seven_day`), that's when the shared one frees up.
**7.2 "It says native cli binary missing for claude (on my Mac)."** The image doesn't have the Claude CLI where Ark expects it. Quick unblock: `export ARK_CLAUDE_EXECUTABLE_PATH=$(which claude)`, or drop a `claude` binary at `/.ark/bin/claude`. Setup scripts are being updated to include it.
**7.3 "Can I use my own Claude account?"** Yes -- the `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` user secret above.
**7.4 "Can we use Cursor?"** In progress

A session stays in the Ready state when Ark can’t move forward because something upstream isn’t available. The most common reasons are:

* **Platform‑wide issue** – if many users see the same problem at the same time, the control plane is likely degraded. In that case stop dispatching new sessions and check the Slack channel for outage notices.
* **SSM rate‑limit** – a flood of sessions can hit the SSM rate‑limit, causing all sessions to queue at Ready. Stop sending new dispatches and wait for the limit to clear.
* **Compute problems** – the box you enrolled may not be healthy, online, or have capacity configured. Enrolling alone isn’t enough; the compute must be registered, have capacity set, and be reachable. Run `ark host doctor` (or the host‑doctor command) to verify connectivity and health.

**What to do**
1. Give it a couple of minutes and retry the dispatch.
2. If the issue is only on your side, check that your compute is healthy and has capacity; run the host‑doctor command.
3. If the problem is affecting many users, stop dispatching and look for a platform‑wide announcement in Slack.
4. When the underlying cause is resolved, the session will move past Ready and continue its lifecycle.

## When it does not work 
Pods sitting `Pending` with `Insufficient cpu` mean the node group is full. Foundry does not scale your cluster, and a node group with no autoscaler stays that size until someone raises it, so a busy fleet stalls silently at that ceiling.
A pod `Pending` with `didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector` is a `nodeSelector` that matches no node: check the label actually on your nodes with `kubectl get nodes --show-labels`, and remember the value must be a quoted string.

Secrets resolve **narrowest first** : user, then team, then tenant, and the first hit for each name wins. A team that sets nothing inherits the tenant default.

After you finish the onboarding steps, you can start using Ark to run your flows.

**1. Discover what you have registered**
- List your flows: `ark flow list` or ask in natural language “list my ark flows”.
- See details of a specific flow: `ark flow show <flow‑name>` or “show the <flow‑name> flow”.
- List your agents: `ark agent list` or “list ark agents”.

**2. Dispatch a session**
- Choose a flow, a workspace that points at your repo, and a compute where it will run.
- In plain English (Claude Code or Cursor with the MCP connected) you can say something like:
  ```
  start my <flow‑name> flow on the <workspace‑name> workspace, summary "<your short description>"
  ```
- The underlying MCP call is:
  ```
  session_lifecycle(op='start', summary='<your description>', flow='<flow‑name>', workspace='<workspace‑name>', compute='<your‑compute>')
  ```
- Only `summary` and `flow` are required; `workspace` and `compute` pin the run to the correct repo and machine.

**3. Watch the session**
- Ask “read that ark session” or “what is the status of my session” to see progress.
- The session will resolve the flow, materialise the workspace on the compute, and launch the first stage’s agent. You’ll see each stage finish and hand off to the next until the final stage completes (e.g., a PR is opened).

**Example end‑to‑end**
```bash
# 1. Register any agents the flow needs
ark agent create myteam-reviewer --from myteam-reviewer.yaml --no-editor --global

# 2. Wire the workspace (repo, secrets, actions, etc.)
ark workspace apply myteam-workspace.yaml

# 3. Validate and register the flow
ark flow validate ./myteam-review.yaml --repo .
ark flow create myteam-review --from myteam-review.yaml

# 4. Dispatch the flow (from Claude Code or Cursor)
# natural‑language example:
#   start my myteam-review flow on the myteam-workspace workspace, summary "review the auth refactor"
# which translates to the MCP call shown above.

# 5. Watch the run
# ask “read that ark session” or “what is the status of my session”.
```

## 1\. Getting started 
**1.1 "What exactly is Ark?"** It's a platform for running supervised AI agents through your software lifecycle, on your own cloud. The agent plans, writes code, runs tests, reviews itself. You dispatch the work, approve the plan, and review the PR at the end. It's not a chatbot and it's not fully autonomous -- it's an engineer's tool with a human gate on the parts that matter.
**1.2 "What all can we use Ark for?"** PR reviews, Developer→PR, turning a Jira ticket into a feature, QA/E2E test generation, security-vuln fixes, and clearing review comments. Start with PR Review -- it's the lowest-risk way to build trust in the output.

## Admin

**how do i add someone to the tenant**

Send the user's email and team name to a tenant admin (listed on the Settings page under Your admins), and the platform team will create their account. Then you control what they can do by granting them roles with the ark grant command. [see: admin]

**why does my team secret keep getting overridden by tenant settings**

Secret resolution follows user → team → tenant order, with the first match winning; if your team sets nothing, it simply inherits tenant defaults. [see: admin]

**can i set jira_base_url at team scope**

No—never override infra values like JIRA_BASE_URL at team scope, as it creates invisible per-team configuration drift that makes Ark appear broken only for that team. [see: admin]

## Adding a user to the tenant 
Account creation (Cognito login + tenant membership) is done by the platform team - send the email and team name (or a .csv for a whole team) to a tenant admin, listed on the **Settings** page under **Your admins**. Once the user exists, you control _what they can do_ with grants:
bash
    
    ark grant <email> --role member                       # tenant-wide member (default scope: tenant)
    ark grant <email> --role team-admin --scope team:<team-slug>
    ark grant list <email>                                # see someone's live grants
    ark grant revoke <grant-id>                           # remove one
Roles: `tenant-admin` | `team-admin` | `member` | `viewer`. Grants are the authority primitive - a team grant covers that team's subtree.

## 3\. Set up a workspace 
A workspace is your project written down once: which repos to clone, which tools to install, which services to run, and which secrets a session needs. It is rebuilt fresh for every session, so an agent starts with a working checkout and a ready toolchain instead of guessing how to build your project.
Start by reading what your tenant already has, rather than authoring one straight away:
bash
    
    ark workspace list
    ark workspace show foundry-platform
Or over MCP:
> list ark workspaces, then show me the foundry-platform workspace
One term to know before your first run: **actions** are named commands a workspace defines, such as `run_unit_tests` or `run_lint`. A stage can call them and read a pass or fail result, which is how a flow gates on your tests rather than on an agent's opinion of them.

2. Choose one of the two snippets it shows (they are alternatives, not a sequence). If you want Ark available in every repo, pick the **plugin one‑liner**; if you only need it for a single repository, pick the **project‑scoped `.mcp.json`**.
3. Copy the generated JSON block (it already contains a fresh user key) into a file named `.cursor/mcp.json`:
   ```json

     "mcpServers": {
       "ark": {
         "type": "http",
         "url": "https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.mlops.pai.mypaytm.com/mcp",
         "headers": {
           "Authorization": "Bearer <YOUR_KEY>"
         }
       }
     }
   }
   ```
   - For a **global** config place this file at `~/.cursor/mcp.json` so Ark is available in any project.
   - For a **project‑scoped** config place it at the repository root as `.cursor/mcp.json`.
4. (Optional) You can add the same entry through Cursor’s UI: open **Tools → Integrations → MCP servers**, add an HTTP server named `ark`, set the URL ending in `/mcp`, and put the header `Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_KEY>`.
5. Verify the connection:
   - In Cursor, open the MCP servers list and confirm that `ark` appears as **connected** and shows the tools (agent, compute, flow, session_lifecycle, workspace, …).
   - Or ask Cursor to run a command like `list ark computes` and see a real answer.
6. If you see an error, make sure:
   - The URL is exactly `https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.mlops.pai.mypaytm.com/mcp` (localhost will not work).
   - The key is a **user** API key (not a machine token, which would return role `worker`).
   - You have not added both the plugin snippet and the project‑scoped snippet – that creates duplicate registrations and can cause “tools fetch failed”.
7. After fixing any issue, restart Claude Code (or the Cursor session) so the new config is picked up.
These steps wire the Ark MCP server into Cursor, letting you run Ark commands (flows, workspaces, etc.) directly from the editor.

You can fix the SSH authentication error that stops workspace preparation by doing the following:

1. **Generate a dedicated, pass‑phrase‑free SSH key** on your machine:
   ```
   ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "ark-bitbucket-$(whoami)" -f ~/.ssh/ark_bitbucket -N ""
   ```
2. **Register the public half with Bitbucket**:
   ```
   cat ~/.ssh/ark_bitbucket.pub
   ```
   Copy the single line that starts with `ssh-ed25519` and add it in Bitbucket under *Settings → SSH keys*.
3. **Verify the key works before adding it to Ark**:
   ```
   ssh -i ~/.ssh/ark_bitbucket -T git@bitbucket.org
   ```
   You should see `authenticated via ssh key.` If you get any other message, fix the key or its registration first.
4. **Add the private key to Ark Secrets**:
   - Open the private key file and copy the whole content, including the `-----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----` and `-----END OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----` lines.
   - Create a secret whose name matches the Bitbucket workspace that holds your repos, e.g. `BITBUCKET_SSH_KEY_PAYTMTEAM` for repos under `bitbucket.org/paytmteam/...`.
   - Scope the secret to **user**, set the type to **ssh‑private‑key**, and paste the private key.
5. **Double‑check the secret name matches the repo URL**. Using the wrong suffix (e.g. `BITBUCKET_SSH_KEY_PAYTMTEAM` for a `paytmmoney` repo) will cause a `Permission denied (publickey)` error.
6. **Run a workspace test to see the real provision and clone phases without an agent**:
   ```
   ark workspace test <your-workspace> --compute <compute-name>
   ```
   Add `--keep` if you want to inspect the prepared tree. The test will stop at the clone step if the SSH credential is still wrong, showing the exact failure.
7. **If the test now passes**, run the normal prepare/dispatch flow (`ark workspace apply …` then dispatch a session). If it still fails, revisit steps 2–5 and ensure the key is not passphrase‑protected, not truncated, and that the Bitbucket account linked to the key has access to the repository.

By following these steps you address the three common causes of clone failures – wrong secret name, an invalid or pass‑phrase‑protected key, or repo visibility – and you can verify the fix before running a full workspace preparation.

Check that you’re in the correct tenant and team – most missing‑compute or missing‑flows issues are just because you’re looking at the wrong scope. Then verify the enrollment from any machine with your Foundry credential:

```bash
ark compute list          # shows all computes your tenant can see
ark compute show <name>   # inspects a specific machine’s health and capacity
```
If `ark compute list` is empty or doesn’t show the box you enrolled, you’re probably in the wrong tenant/team. Once the compute is visible, your flows will also appear when you’re in the same tenant/team.

In Ark:
- **Compute** is the machine or runtime where the work actually runs. It’s the target that executes the session’s agents and actions.
- **Workspace** is the collection of your code and tooling – the repos, secrets, named actions, and any other resources that the flow needs. It materialises per session so the flow can clone the repo, install tools, and run commands.
- **Flow** is the delivery process itself. It’s a DAG of stages, each of which is either an agent or a workspace action, and defines how work moves from one stage to the next (including back‑edges for re‑work). A flow runs *against* a workspace on a compute.
Thus, a compute provides the execution environment, a workspace supplies the code and tools, and a flow describes *what* to do with that code on that compute.

```bash

1. Install the Ark CLI and confirm you are logged in:
```bash
ark --version
ark auth whoami   # should show your email, role and tenant
``` (see chunks 19, 24)

2. Obtain a user API key (from Settings → API Keys) – this is the credential you will use for enrollment.

**Option A – One‑command enrollment script**
```bash
export API_KEY=ark_t-..._xxx          # your user API key
export MACHINE_NAME=my-box          # the name you want for the host
./ark-enroll-host.sh                # runs the installer, logs in, mints a host token, installs bun & Claude Code, registers arkd as a service and starts it (chunks 3‑7)
```
The script is idempotent; re‑running it rotates the token safely (chunks 3, 7). If you need to run it on a machine without sudo, use the `--launchd` flag on macOS (chunks 8‑9).

**Option B – Manual enrollment**
```bash
# on the target machine, with the CLI installed and you logged in as the user who should own the host
ark host enroll <MACHINE_NAME> --isolation direct --detach   # or --launchd on macOS, --systemd on Linux for a persistent service (chunks 10, 8‑9)
```
`--isolation` can be `direct` or `docker`. `--detach` backgrounds the daemon (won’t survive reboot); use `--launchd` or `--systemd` for a long‑lived box.

**Enrolling on someone else’s behalf** (admin or team admin mints the token, then the owner starts the daemon):
```bash
# Admin step – mint token
ark host enroll <MACHINE_NAME>        # reads token into ~/.ark/host/registered-host/<MACHINE_NAME>/token
# Send the token securely to the machine’s owner (chunk 1, 11, 16)

# Owner step – place token and start daemon
mkdir -p ~/.ark/host/registered-host/<MACHINE_NAME>
printf '%s' '<token>' > ~/.ark/host/registered-host/<MACHINE_NAME>/token
chmod 600 ~/.ark/host/registered-host/<MACHINE_NAME>/token
ark host start <MACHINE_NAME> --detach   # no admin credential needed (chunks 1, 16)
```

3. Verify the host is registered and reachable:
```bash
ark compute list               # shows the host if it has checked in (chunk 15)
ark compute show <MACHINE_NAME>
ark host status <MACHINE_NAME>   # local check; true enrollment is confirmed by the compute list (chunk 15)
```
If the host shows up in `ark compute list`, it is successfully enrolled and ready for dispatching sessions.

## Capacity and admission 
Admission control decides how much work a box will accept before it queues the rest, and it is on by default. When a compute declares no `capacity`, Foundry derives a conservative one from the instance size at 85% headroom, reserving the rest for the OS, `arkd`, and the agent runtime. An `m` box (8 vCPU, 32 GB) therefore admits against roughly 27Gi and 680% CPU.
An adopted box carries no size, because Foundry did not choose its instance type and will not invent one, so declaring capacity is not optional there: until you do, a workspace that declares a `resource_budget` is refused on it with a message naming exactly this. A workspace declaring no budget is not gated at all, so an uncapped adopted box will accept work regardless.

To let Ark pods reach Jira (or Bitbucket) you need a stable egress IP that the Atlassian services can whitelist. Fix it by:
1. Add a NAT gateway with a fixed public IP (or a set of fixed IPs) to the compute pool and any EC2 boxes used by Ark.
2. Route all outbound traffic from the Ark pods/EC2s through that NAT gateway so the source IP is the fixed one.
3. Submit a whitelisting request to the Jira/Bitbucket admin (or the internal ticket RMB‑3516) that adds the NAT gateway’s public IP(s) to the Atlassian IP allow‑list.
4. Ensure the security group attached to the compute resources allows outbound HTTPS (port 443) to the Atlassian endpoints—VPC peering alone is not enough.
Once the NAT IP is approved, Ark’s pods can call the Jira MCP over REST without needing a VPN.

Here’s the full onboarding checklist for Ark, in the order the docs say you should do it:

1. **Install the CLI** – open the Onboarding tab in the web UI, click the *Install the CLI* card, run the generated one‑liner (or download the binary) and then run:
   ```
   ark --version
   ark auth whoami
   ```
   to confirm the binary is on your PATH and you’re authenticated.
2. **Get access and connect** – after the CLI is installed, run `ark auth whoami` and verify it prints your email, role, and the expected tenant.
3. **Add your personal credentials** – set up the SSH key that lets Ark talk to your repos:
   ```
   ssh -i ~/.ssh/ark_bitbucket -T git@bitbucket.org
   ```
   (this proves your secrets are in place).
4. **Join your team and add secrets** – make sure you belong to the right team/tenant, then add any required repository secrets in the Ark UI.
5. **Enroll compute** – either have your DevOps create a compute box for the team or enroll a machine you already own (see the *One‑command enrollment* page). The compute must be healthy before you can run a session.
6. **Run your first session** – dispatch a session (e.g. `ark flow list` to see available flows, then `ark flow create …` or ask Cursor/Claude Code to “start an ark session”). You should receive a session ID and see the run progress to its final stage.
7. **Run the workspace doctor** – after the compute is up, run the workspace‑doctor command (shown on the onboarding pages) to validate your workspace configuration.
8. **Link the Slack bot** – finish the onboarding flow by linking the Slack bot so you get notifications and can approve plans directly from Slack.
9. **First PR review** – use the built‑in PR‑review flow to create a pull request, review it, and merge. This is the lowest‑risk way to see Ark in action.
10. **Developer→PR and Jira→PR** – once the PR‑review works, you can run the full Developer→PR flow and later tie Jira tickets to PRs.

Following these steps in order will get you from a fresh account to a running Ark session that you can watch and review.

# Getting Started with Ark 
You have an account and the `ark` MCP connected in Claude Code or Cursor. This page is the first run: it takes you from a connected editor to a session you dispatched, watched, and reviewed, in seven ordered steps. Every step is a small command you can run and read the answer to, so you are never guessing whether the last one worked.
The four nouns everything is built from are a **compute** (where a run happens), a **workspace** (your project made real: repos, tools, secrets, actions), a **flow** (the delivery process written down as stages), and a **session** (one run of a flow on a workspace on a compute). Steps 2 through 4 pick each of the first three; step 5 puts them together into a session.

You need a few prerequisites and then you create the pool via the compute MCP (or its JSON‑RPC endpoint).  The required pieces are:

1. **Permissions** – you must be a tenant‑admin (or have the `compute.admin` role) because creating a pool is a tenant‑level action.
2. **CLI and cloud setup** – an `ark` CLI that is signed in to your control‑plane, the AWS CLI configured for the account that owns the EKS cluster, and `kubectl` pointing at that cluster.
3. **Cluster access** – the tenant must be allowed to target the cluster (if the tenant is locked to specific clusters you’ll get a *Tenant "<id>" is not permitted to target k8s cluster "<key>"* error).
4. **Namespace** – the K8s namespace in which the pods will be created.
5. **Image** – the container image for the pods.  Using `image: 'self'` makes the pods use the same image that the Ark CLI is running, otherwise supply a full image reference.
6. **Control‑plane URL** – the URL the pod’s `arkd` will dial back to (e.g. `https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.mlops.pai.mypaytm.com`).
7. **Resources** – CPU and memory requests for the pod (e.g. `cpu: '2', memory: '8Gi'`).
8. **Optional cross‑account details** – if the EKS cluster is in a different AWS account, provide `roleArn` and `externalId`; otherwise omit them.
9. **Capacity settings** – `capacity.cpu`, `capacity.memory`, and `capacity.max_sessions` if you want to limit concurrency for the pool.

**Creation steps**
```bash
# 1. Build a JSON payload (or equivalent RPC call) that includes the fields above
compute({
  op: 'pool_create',
  name: 'risk-eks',
  compute_kind: 'k8s',
  isolation_kind: 'direct',
  config: {
    cluster: {
      kind: 'eks',
      region: 'ap-south-1',
      clusterName: 'risk-agents',
      roleArn: 'arn:aws:iam::<your-account>:role/ark-cross-account-<slug>',
      externalId: '<your external id>'
    },
    namespace: 'foundry-platform',
    image: 'self',
    controlPlaneUrl: 'https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.mlops.pai.mypaytm.com',
    resources: { cpu: '2', memory: '8Gi' },
    nodeSelector: { role: 'agents' },
    tolerations: [{ key: 'role', operator: 'Equal', value: 'agents', effect: 'NoSchedule' }],
    capacity: { memory: '32Gi', cpu: '800', max_sessions: 4 }
  }
})
```
The CLI itself has no flag for an EKS ref, so you typically send the payload via the compute MCP tool or its `compute/pool/create` RPC endpoint.

**Verify**
```bash
ark compute list          # shows the new pool row (status will be empty)
ark compute show risk-eks # displays capacity, occupancy, etc.
```
Then start a test session:
```bash
ark session start --flow bare-auto --compute risk-eks --summary "k8s smoke test"
```
Watch the pod appear in the namespace with:
```bash
kubectl -n <namespace> get pods -w -l ark.dev/kind=k8s
```
If the pod shows up and the session proceeds, the pool is correctly set up.

**Key points**: a k8s pool is always cold (no warm floor), its `status` field is empty, and you control concurrency via the `capacity` fields rather than `min`/`max` limits.

# Creating Kubernetes compute 
A `k8s` compute is not a machine. It is a pool row holding the cluster, the namespace, the pod image and the pod's resource limits, and every dispatch cuts one pod from it for one session. The pod runs `arkd` as its main container and dials out to the control plane, so nothing reaches into your cluster: no inbound route, no `kubectl port-forward`, no kubeconfig read at dispatch time. When the session ends the pod is deleted.
Because the pod is created per dispatch, a k8s pool is always cold. Setting a warm floor is rejected outright with `cannot be warm (min must be 0)`. There is nothing to keep warm.

# Creating EC2 compute 
An `ec2` compute is usually a machine Foundry owns end to end: it launches the instance in your AWS account, installs `arkd` on it over SSM, stops it when it goes idle, and terminates it when you destroy the row. The same kind can also adopt a box you already run, in which case Foundry installs `arkd` and nothing else, as below. That is the difference from [registering a machine you already own](/onboarding/registering-compute), where the box dials in and Foundry never touches its lifecycle.

Four numbers decide pod size and throughput, and none of them substitutes for another:
Field| What it sets  
---|---

# Set up Cursor 
Cursor shows up in Foundry in two unrelated ways, and this page covers both.
The first is Cursor as your editor: it connects to the control plane's MCP server and gets the `ark` toolbox, so you can dispatch sessions, inspect flows and steer runs without leaving Cursor. The second is Cursor as a **runtime** , one of the harnesses Foundry dispatches agents onto, alongside the `claude-agent` and `pi-dev` families and their `-pi-inference` gateway variants. In that mode nobody is sitting in the editor at all: a stage runs on Cursor's agent SDK, on an EC2 box, a registered host or in a Kubernetes pod, and reports back like any other stage.
If you only want to drive Foundry from your editor, read to the end of Use it and then skip to Notes and gotchas. If you are running flows on the Cursor harness, the sections from Cursor as an agent harness onward are the ones you need.

Alternatively, you can use the script that downloads the CLI to a temp file, verifies it, and moves it into place, and then re-adds the marketplace with the current token and installs the plugin. The script is the full path when you want to move the CLI binary forward too. ## Why it works this way 
Two steps look indirect on purpose.
The CLI downloads to a temp file and then moves into place rather than writing straight to `~/.ark/bin/ark`. A direct write would follow a symlink and overwrite whatever the link points at; the move replaces the entry itself.
The plugin marketplace is re-added with the current token rather than updated in place, and it is never removed first. The marketplace URL embeds whichever token was current when you installed it, so after a key rotation or a tenant switch a plain `claude plugin marketplace update` keeps presenting the stale token and returns a 401 with no way to recover in place. Re-adding under the same `ark` name overwrites the stored source, token and all, which refreshes the credential without uninstalling anything. Once you are on the current release, applying a tenant workspace takes an explicit `--namespace <token>`: `ark workspace apply <file> --namespace <token>` prepends the token to the YAML's `name:`, so the stored name is `<token>-<name>`. An `ec2` compute is usually a machine Foundry owns end to end: it launches the instance in your AWS account, installs `arkd` on it over SSM, stops it when it goes idle, and terminates it when you destroy the row. records.answer: To set up Cursor with Ark MCP, add the Ark MCP server to Cursor by copying the generated config from the Onboarding tab's 'Connect Claude Code (superpowers)' card into `.cursor/mcp.json`, either globally at `~/.cursor/mcp.json` or project-scoped at the repo root. Use a global config at `~/.cursor/mcp.json` to make `ark` available in every project, or a project-scoped `.cursor/mcp.json` at the repo root to scope it to one repo. The URL must be `https://ark.internal.ap-south-1.platform.mlops.pai.mypaytm.com/mcp` with the `Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_KEY>` header. You can also add it through Cursor's own settings: find the MCP servers list and add an HTTP server named `ark`, with the URL ending in `/mcp` and the `Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_KEY>` header. Then, verify your Ark connection is working by opening Cursor's MCP servers list and checking that `ark` shows as connected with its tools listed, or ask Cursor to 'list ark computes' and watch a real answer come back.

### 0. Make Ark Reliable

**Goal:** Stop the outages before we add anything new.

- Stop 503s: credential-refresh grant for the weekly DB password rotation, plus event-consumer backpressure.
- Redis recovery, and managed EC2 or EKS instead of laptops.

- Do not kill a healthy long build, and surface no silent hangs.
- Pause and resume on a rate limit, and preserve work on every kill.
- Reduce UI polling, keep auth stable under load, and deliver Slack alarms.

**Done when:** No unannounced outage over 5 minutes, failures are fast and clear, arkd holds at normal load, healthy builds keep running, no silent hangs, the UI stays fast, no repeated logouts, no lost work, and alerts fire before users report.

records.answer: You can enroll a compute host on Ark by running `ark host enroll <name>` on the machine itself, signed in with the credential whose rung you want the box on. This mints a token, writes it to the host's token file, and starts `arkd` dialing the control plane. Alternatively, an admin can mint the token and send it to the machine's owner, who can then start the daemon with `ark host start <name> --detach`. If you are enrolling on behalf of someone else, you can use `ark-enroll-host.sh` which automates the enrollment process. Before enrolling, ensure you have an Ark API key and the machine has a network path to the control plane over 443.

## Capacity and admission 
Admission control decides how much work a box will accept before it queues the rest, and it is on by default. When a compute declares no `capacity`, Foundry derives a conservative one from the instance size at 85% headroom, reserving the rest for the OS, `arkd`, and the agent runtime. An `m` box (8 vCPU, 32 GB) therefore admits against roughly 27Gi and 680% CPU.
An adopted box carries no size, because Foundry did not choose its instance type and will not invent one, so declaring capacity is not optional there: until you do, a workspace that declares a `resource_budget` is refused on it with a message naming exactly this. A workspace declaring no budget is not gated at all, so an uncapped adopted box will accept work regardless.

You have an account and the `ark` MCP connected in Claude Code or Cursor. This page is the first run: it takes you from a connected editor to a session you dispatched, watched, and reviewed, in seven ordered steps. Every step is a small command you can run and read the answer to, so you are never guessing whether the last one worked.
The four nouns everything is built from are a **compute** (where a run happens), a **workspace** (your project made real: repos, tools, secrets, actions), a **flow** (the delivery process written down as stages), and a **session** (one run of a flow on a workspace on a compute). Steps 2 through 4 pick each of the first three; step 5 puts them together into a session.

# Ark -- FAQ & Troubleshooting 
A living doc, written by engineers who onboarded the first teams. If something here is wrong or out of date, fix it -- that's the whole point. Sourced from the teams' own onboarding threads (Foundry Slack + WhatsApp) and the platform engineers who answer them day to day. Questions are kept in the voice people actually ask them.

records.answer: To set up a k8s compute pool for ark, you need to create a pool with the `ark compute pool create` command, specifying the compute kind as `k8s`, the namespace, image, control plane URL, resources, and node selector. The pool is always cold, and setting a warm floor is rejected. The `capacity` section is used to size the pod and set the admission ledger's ceiling for the whole pool row. You can use the `compute` MCP tool or the `compute/pool/create` RPC endpoint to create the pool. Use `ark compute update` to set the rest of the launch config on the pool afterwards.

A `k8s` compute is not a machine. It is a pool row holding the cluster, the namespace, the pod image and the pod's resource limits, and every dispatch cuts one pod from it for one session. The pod runs `arkd` as its main container and dials out to the control plane, so nothing reaches into your cluster: no inbound route, no `kubectl port-forward`, no kubeconfig read at dispatch time. `config.sidecarResources`| Charged once per declared service, plus one for DinD, in the same pod  
`config.capacity`| The admission ledger's ceiling for the whole pool row  
The pod total is `arkd` plus every sidecar, and that total has to fit on one node after daemonsets and kube-reserved take their share, which is meaningfully less than the instance spec suggests. A workspace that asks for slightly more than a node can give never schedules at all

From there that admin unlocks the rest for the team: they onboard everyone else, register the team's compute, and set the team's secrets, without the platform team in the loop for each step.
Ark has four roles:
  - **Member** is the everyday role. A member creates flows, agents, and workspaces, runs sessions, uses shared secrets, and edits or deletes what they created. Most people are members.
  - **Team-admin** runs one team. It does everything a member can, and manages its own team's shared resources and secrets. Its authority covers that team and its sub-teams, and nothing outside them.
  - **Tenant-admin** runs the whole tenant: onboard anyone, manage every team, register compute, an

If you must register a Mac, scope it to **your own user** and not to the team.

- Session-scoped SSH keys, and automated cross-account VPC peering.

`capacity.cpu` is a percent integer where one core is `100`, so `600` is six cores. Four numbers decide pod size and throughput, and none of them substitutes for another:
Field| What it sets

Onboarding a team comes down to one person. The platform team creates the accounts and gives one person a tenant-admin grant. Make sure you’re in the correct tenant/team, then verify the compute is registered and healthy, and that it has capacity set so it appears in listings.
1. Confirm you are on the right tenant and team (wrong tenant/team is the most common cause).
2. Run `ark compute list` to see if your machine shows up.
3. If it doesn’t, on the machine run `ark host status <name>` and ensure `arkd` is running and the box has capacity configured.
4. If the host is not healthy or capacity is missing, re‑enroll it with `ark host enroll <name>` and set its capacity.
5. After the compute appears in `ark compute list`, your flows should also be visible in the same tenant/team.

# Onboarding

**Goal:** Stop the outages before we add anything new.

- Stop 503s: credential-refresh grant for the weekly DB password rotation, plus event-consumer backpressure.

An `ec2` compute is usually a machine Foundry owns end to end: it launches the instance in your AWS account, installs `arkd` on it over SSM, stops it when it goes idle, and terminates it when you destroy the row. The same kind can also adopt a box you already run, in which case Foundry installs `arkd` and nothing else, as below. That is the difference from [registering a machine you already own](/onboarding/registering-compute), where the box dials in and Foundry never touches its lifecycle.
You create it in one of two shapes. A **dedicated box** is a single named instance your team's sessions land on, which is what most teams start with. A **pool** is a blueprint that cuts a fresh instance per session up to a ceiling you set, which is what you want once several people dispatch at once. Do this from a terminal where `ark` is on your PATH. All three commands read from a YAML file.
**Step 1 - Define your agents.** Write each agent as a YAML file. ## Capacity and admission 
Admission control decides how much work a box will accept before it queues the rest, and it is on by default. When a compute declares no `capacity`, Foundry derives a conservative one from the instance size at 85% headroom, reserving the rest for the OS, `arkd`, and the agent runtime. An `m` box (8 vCPU, 32 GB) therefore admits against roughly 27Gi and 680% CPU.
An adopted box carries no size, because Foundry did not choose its instance type and will not invent one, so declaring capacity is not optional there: until you do, a workspace that declares a `resource_budget` is refused on it with a message naming exactly this. A workspace declaring no budget is not gated at all, so an uncapped adopted box will accept work regardless.
Declare it explicitly whenever you want a different ceiling, and always on an adopted box:

### 0. Make Ark Reliable

**Goal:** Stop the outages before we add anything new.

- Stop 503s: credential-refresh grant for the weekly DB password rotation, plus event-consumer backpressure.
- Redis recovery, and managed EC2 or EKS instead of laptops.
- Team-scoped compute and credentials, with pre-flight prerequisite checks.
- Prevent an arkd disconnect from stranding a run; detect machine loss and recover.
- Do not kill a healthy long build, and surface no silent hangs.
- Pause and resume on a rate limit, and preserve work on every kill.
- Reduce UI polling, keep auth stable under load, and deliver Slack alarms.

**Done when:** No unannounced outage over 5 minutes, failures are fast and clear, arkd holds at normal load, healthy builds keep running, no silent hangs, the UI stays fast, no repeated logouts, no lost work, and alerts fire before users report.

## 12\. For DevOps / platform 
**12.1 "What are the enrollment best practices?"** Enroll to the right team, bake the standard toolchain into the image, verify with host doctor before go-live.

# Getting Started with Ark 
You have an account and the `ark` MCP connected in Claude Code or Cursor. This page is the first run: it takes you from a connected editor to a session you dispatched, watched, and reviewed, in seven ordered steps. Every step is a small command you can run and read the answer to, so you are never guessing whether the last one worked.
The four nouns everything is built from are a **compute** (where a run happens), a **workspace** (your project made real: repos, tools, secrets, actions), a **flow** (the delivery process written down as stages), and a **session** (one run of a flow on a workspace on a compute). Steps 2 through 4 pick each of the first three; step 5 puts them together into a session.
Most people drive Ark from Claude Code in plain English, so each step below shows the natural-language MCP phrasing alongside the `ark` CL

Only `summary` and `flow` are required; `workspace` and `compute` are what pin the run to your repo and where it executes (list computes with "list ark computes"). Add `ticket='PAI-1234'` to link a Jira issue, or `autonomy='read-only'` for a dry look.

`whoami` prints the user, role and tenant the credential resolves to. Read it now rather than later: every command on the following pages acts as that identity.
